sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll understand what GitHub Actions does, how to read a YAML workflow file, and how to use Claude to generate workflows for your projects.

## What is GitHub Actions?

GitHub Actions is a CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) system built directly into GitHub. It runs automated tasks in response to git events — pushing code, opening a pull request, merging a branch, creating a tag.

When you push code, GitHub Actions can automatically:
- Run your tests and fail the PR if tests don't pass
- Check code style and formatting
- Deploy to a server
- Send a notification
- Open an issue if something breaks
- Run an AI code review

The configuration lives in your repository at `.github/workflows/` as YAML files. Every file in that folder is a separate workflow.

## Reading a Workflow File

Here is a minimal GitHub Actions workflow that runs on every push:

name: Run Tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Check out code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

Let's break down the key parts:

- `name` — what this workflow is called (appears in the GitHub UI)
- `on` — what triggers the workflow. `push` means every push to main. `pull_request` means every PR targeting main.
- `jobs` — the list of jobs to run. You can have multiple jobs that run in parallel or sequence.
- `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` — every job runs on a fresh virtual machine. The VM is temporary and destroyed after the job.
- `steps` — the list of steps within a job. Steps run in order.
- `uses: actions/checkout@v4` — this runs a pre-built action that checks out your code onto the VM
- `run: npm test` — runs a shell command

You don't need to memorize the syntax. Claude can generate any workflow file you need — you just need to be able to read and understand what it produces.

**The best use of AI with GitHub Actions:** Describe what you want in plain English, get the YAML from Claude, then ask Claude to explain each part so you understand what you're committing. Never commit an Actions workflow you can't explain — a misconfigured workflow can expose secrets or run unintended commands.

## An AI-Powered Code Review Workflow

Here is a workflow that runs an AI code review whenever a pull request is opened or updated:

name: AI Code Review

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Check out code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: AI Code Review
        uses: anc95/ChatGPT-CodeReview@main
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}

**Note on API keys:** This particular workflow uses an OpenAI API key (`OPENAI_API_KEY`) — this is one place in the course that uses OpenAI. If you don't have an OpenAI account, search the GitHub Actions Marketplace for "Claude code review" for an Anthropic-native alternative. The concept (AI review on every PR) is the same regardless of which model runs it.

To add secrets to GitHub: repo Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret.

sections.title: Generate a GitHub Actions Workflow
sections.content:
You'll use Claude Code to generate a custom GitHub Actions workflow for your project, then push it to your GitHub repository.

**Step 1 — Describe what you want**
1. Launch `claude` in your `ai-course-projects` folder
2. Ask: `Generate a GitHub Actions workflow YAML file for my project. The workflow should:
- Run on every push to main and on every pull request
- Check out the code
- Set up Node.js 20
- Run 'npm install'
- Run any .js files in the exercises/ folder with node to check they don't crash
- Post a comment on pull requests summarizing what ran`
3. Review what Claude proposes

**Step 2 — Understand the output**
Before accepting, ask Claude: `Explain each section of this workflow file. What does 'runs-on: ubuntu-latest' mean? What is GITHUB_TOKEN and where does it come from?`

Make sure you understand:
- What event triggers it
- What the VM does
- What secrets are needed (if any)
- What the expected output is

**Step 3 — Create the file**
1. Ask Claude to create the file: `Create .github/workflows/ci.yml with this workflow`
2. Claude will create the directory and file
3. Open the file in VS Code and read every line

**Step 4 — Push and test**
1. Stage and commit: `git add .github/` then commit with a message like `ci: add GitHub Actions workflow`
2. Push to your GitHub repository
3. Go to github.com → your repo → the **Actions** tab
4. Watch your workflow run (first run appears within 30-60 seconds)
5. Click the workflow run to see the step-by-step output

**What to observe:** Every future push to this repo will automatically run this workflow. The green checkmark or red X on each commit and PR is the CI system giving you instant feedback.

sections.title: Workshop A — First GitHub Actions Workflow
sections.content:
Create a GitHub Actions workflow that uses Claude for code review.

**Step 1 — Create a GitHub repository** (or use an existing one).

**Step 2 — Create `.github/workflows/ai-review.yml`:**
```yaml
name: AI Code Quality Check
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run linter
        run: |
          npm install --save-dev eslint
          npx eslint . --ext .js,.ts || true
```

**Step 3 — Commit and push.** Create a PR to trigger the workflow.

**Step 4 — View the workflow run** in GitHub Actions. What does it report?

**Step 5 — Ask Claude Code** to improve the workflow: "Make this workflow also run tests and report results as a PR comment."

sections.title: Workshop B — AI-Powered CI Pipeline
sections.content:
Build a CI pipeline that includes AI quality gates.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude Code** to design a complete CI pipeline for your project type:
```
Design a GitHub Actions CI pipeline for a [Python/Node.js/etc] project that:
1. Runs on every PR
2. Checks: linting, tests, security scan
3. Posts a summary comment on the PR
4. Blocks merge if tests fail
5. Is fast (target: under 3 minutes)

Write the complete workflow YAML file.
```

**Step 2 — Review the generated YAML** carefully before using it — understand every step.

**Step 3 — Implement the workflow** in a real repository.

**Step 4 — Create a PR to trigger it.** Did all checks pass?

**Step 5 — Mandatory review:** Ask: *"Review this GitHub Actions workflow. What security risks exist? What steps could be made faster? What important checks are missing?"*

sections.title: Workshop C — GitHub Actions Security
sections.content:
Learn to write secure GitHub Actions workflows.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** *"What are the most common security vulnerabilities in GitHub Actions workflows? For each, show an example of the vulnerable pattern and the secure alternative."*

**Step 2 — Audit your workflow from Workshop B:**
- Are you pinning action versions by hash? (not @v3 but @sha256:...)
- Are secrets passed via environment variables, not command args?
- Is the GITHUB_TOKEN permission scoped to minimum needed?
- Are you running code from fork PRs safely?

**Step 3 — Fix at least one security issue** in your workflow.

**Step 4 — Ask Claude Code** to write a more secure version of the workflow with all security best practices applied.

**Step 5 — Compare the two workflows.** What changed? Are the secure practices meaningfully more complex?

sections.title: Workshop D — Automated Deployment Pipeline
sections.content:
Build a deployment pipeline that uses AI for deployment safety checks.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude Code** to design a deployment workflow:
```
Design a GitHub Actions deployment workflow for [describe your project and hosting]:
1. Triggered on merge to main
2. Runs full test suite
3. Builds the production artifact
4. Deploys to [staging/production]
5. Runs a smoke test after deployment
6. Rolls back if smoke test fails
7. Notifies [Slack/email] on success or failure
```

**Step 2 — Implement the staging deployment step** (even if you don't have a real staging environment, create the YAML structure).

**Step 3 — Add a smoke test job** that checks the deployed application is responding correctly.

**Step 4 — Mandatory review:** Ask Claude: *"Review this deployment pipeline. What could go wrong in the rollback step? What if deployment partially succeeds before the failure? How do we handle a failed deployment state?"*

sections.question: A GitHub Actions workflow runs `npm install && npm test` on every PR. A malicious contributor submits a PR that adds code to package.json's postinstall script. What is the risk?
options: No risk — GitHub Actions is sandboxed
The postinstall script runs during npm install and could execute malicious code in your CI environment, potentially exfiltrating secrets
The PR would be automatically rejected
npm install never runs custom scripts in CI
sections.explanation: Running untrusted code (from external PRs) in CI is a real attack vector. The postinstall hook runs during npm install — if a malicious PR modifies package scripts, those scripts execute in your CI environment, which has access to repository secrets and deployment credentials. Mitigation: never run workflows triggered by pull_request_target with write permissions or access to secrets for untrusted PRs; review workflow triggers carefully.

sections.question: Your CI workflow takes 15 minutes to run. Every PR triggers the full pipeline. What is the highest-impact change to make it faster?
options: Buy more expensive GitHub Actions runners
Parallelise independent jobs (linting, testing, building) and add caching for dependencies (node_modules, pip packages)
Run only the tests related to changed files
sections.explanation: The two highest-ROI CI optimisations: (1) parallelisation — run lint, test, and build as separate jobs that run simultaneously instead of sequentially; and (2) caching — use actions/cache for node_modules, pip packages, Go modules, etc., so dependencies aren't reinstalled on every run. Together these can reduce a 15-minute pipeline to 4-5 minutes without skipping any checks.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 10-6.** You can now generate, read, and deploy GitHub Actions workflows using AI. CI/CD is no longer just for large teams — it takes 10 minutes to add automation to any project. Next: designing your personal AI workflow system.
